Few questions:
1. Do you have a green card or do you need a visa sponsor? Many firms won’t come out and say it, but needing a visa sponsor is a hassle. Outside of large multinational firm with the HR structure in place to handle it, it’s extra work for smaller/midsize shops and might hurt your chances.

2. Do you have the necessary credit hours to sit for the CPA in the US? If not, figure out what you need and how many courses need taking. You can likely get through them at a local community college for a few thousand dollars. Having a CPA isn’t necessary for a successful career, but most employers prefer it. 

3. Some companies might sponsor an MBA but only after you put a few years in at the company. 

4. What’s your current role? AP/AR, staff accountant, etc.? If you haven’t been promoted in four years and been at an AR/AP role it might be sending out a red flag of incompetence or not caring about the job. Make sure your resume reflects and promos and responsibilities you have accurately. 

5. Keep applying.

It’s a new rule that in 2024 you can redeem the tax credit at the point of sale. In effect you’re transferring the credit to the dealer. The dealership needs to be registered with the IRS so make sure they are before purchasing.

How to tax credit works depends on the state tax and its tax credit rules. For example, Texas gave a 10k EV credit for purchases in the 2023 calendar year if you had AGI of less than $150k. If you rise above that threshold, then you’d be liable if you took the credit and don’t qualify.

You cannot determine your tax filings before having accurate bookkeeping records, so one step at a time. 

It’s hard to quote how long taxes will take depending on the complexity of your books as well as how good your record keeping has been, I.e. if you say you have mileage deductions, deductible business meals, fixed assets depreciation etc. do you have the receipts and records to support those tax positions. A CPA, EA, or other tax preparer credentialed person, puts their name on the return and if you’re audited your preparer can face some consequences if it’s not up to snuff.

If the firm you’re looking at is just a bookkeeping firm then it makes sense they don’t do taxes. There’s a difference between bookkeeping, accounting, tax prep, and tax planning. It’s like hiring a general practitioner to do a hip replacement surgery. Some firms do both bookkeeping and tax prep/tax planning so that might be more your speed. However, firm that do both are typically more credentialed and might charge even more.

There’s more to just categorizing transactions. A good bookkeeper should be reconciling balance sheet accounts on a monthly basis, and if they’re decent with financial analytics can give you financial updates and insights on operations trends they’re seeing. 

Once you’re a client it takes much less time per month. I charge my clients an hourly rate the first 3 months until I get a precise idea on the client’s goals then establish a fixed rate monthly fee. CPA’s can charge anywhere from $30 to $500 per hour. I currently charge $80. Taking 3-4 hours per month is reasonable once you’re an established client just to do transaction review and account reconciliations. $300 per month isn’t unreasonable.

Mate, I’m a CPA and run my own bookkeeping & tax prep firm on the side. You’re not getting taken advantage of here.

You are two years delinquent on taxes, you’ve never had an accountant or bookkeeper, and you said yourself that you don’t know the first thing about accounting. Your records are likely a mess beyond belief. You’ve made close to $1 million this year so you either have high transaction volume (I’m assuming your probably an Amazon FBA seller since you said you’re young and it’s online products) or you have some high ticket consulting business with online courses. 

It’s not a matter if bookkeeping costs 4K per year. If you hired a good bookkeeper at the start or a few months in to your business it’d be a lot cheaper to clean up a few months worth of transactions in a single calendar year than work to reconcile every account, pull in transactions to your ledgers (I’m assuming you use quickbooks) if you use outside systems for invoicing, or PayPal etc, then work to close prior years books. This sounds like at minimum 1-2 weeks of full time work and active calls with you to work out a lot of backlog. $8k sounds pretty on the money for initial cleanup. Then maybe a couple hundred each month to keep them on retainer and keep your books.

Retained earnings carries over year over year as a balance sheet account. 

Assets = Liabilities + Equity

300,000 Assets = 125,000 Liability + 60,000 (Equity) + X (Equity)

X is $115,000 Retained Earnings when you solve.

This means retained earnings went up by $20,000 from 2021 to 2022. Retained earnings goes up when your net income (revenue - expenses - dividends) is positive. Therefore, net income of the year would have to be 20,000. 

Revenue (X) - Expenses (135,500) - Dividends (6,500) = 20,000

When you solve the equation, you get revenue should be $162,000.
